# 2025 Enderlin Tornado

On the night of June 20, 2025, a large and extremely violent EF5 tornado moved through rural Cass County near the community of Enderlin in southeastern North Dakota. Part of a larger outbreak and derecho sequence that occurred across the northern Great Plains between June 19 and 22, the tornado was the first to be rated EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale since the tornado that struck Moore, Oklahoma, on May 20, 2013, ending a 12-year period without EF5 tornadoes in the United States. The Enderlin tornado was also the first F5 or EF5 tornado to occur in North Dakota since June 20, 1957, exactly 68 years prior. It killed three people and caused extensive damage across a path spanning approximately 19.5 kilometers (12.1 miles), making it the deadliest tornado to strike the state since an F4 tornado hit Elgin in 1978.

The tornado initially touched down at 11:02 p.m. Central Daylight Time (CDT) south of Enderlin with weak EF0 intensity. As it moved northeastward, it rapidly intensified, eventually reaching EF5 strength with wind speeds exceeding 210 miles per hour (340 kilometers per hour). Initial surveys classified the tornado as a high-end EF3 with estimated winds of 160 mph (260 km/h), but additional analysis revealed extraordinary damage to a freight train, leading to an upgrade to EF5 on October 6, 2025. The upgrade was based on forensic engineering analysis of derailed and lofted train cars, a methodology developed through research by the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University in Canada.

### Meteorological Synopsis

In the days preceding the outbreak, favorable atmospheric conditions developed across the northern Great Plains. On June 15, the Storm Prediction Center issued a Day 6 outlook forecasting a shortwave trough that would move into the upper Mississippi River Valley with strong instability and deep-layer wind shear expected across the region. As June 20 approached, a potent low-level jet (LLJ) developed after sunset, providing additional wind shear to support significant tornado activity during the nighttime hours.

The tornado occurred within the larger context of a significant derecho and tornado outbreak sequence. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued for parts of southwestern and south-central North Dakota at 3:45 p.m. CDT as thunderstorms began developing in eastern Montana. The environment was exceptionally favorable for severe weather, with potential for both violent tornadoes and significant damaging winds. The derecho portion of the outbreak produced widespread wind gusts exceeding 60 mph across the region, with some locations experiencing gusts over 100 mph.

### Storm Track and Damage

The tornado touched down approximately 1 mile southwest of Liberty, North Dakota, south of Enderlin, at 11:02 p.m. CDT. Initially, it caused only EF0 damage, snapping tree branches and creating minor damage across County Road 55 through open fields as it moved northeastward. The tornado then widened and intensified as it crossed County Road 55.

At the corner of 136th Avenue Southeast and County Road 136, the tornado struck the ADM Edible Bean Specialties facility at EF2 intensity, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding. This industrial facility marks a clear progression in tornado intensity along the damage path.

The tornado then rapidly intensified as it continued northeastward, reaching catastrophic EF5 intensity as it crossed a Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) rail line southeast of Enderlin. At this location, the tornado derailed 33 freight train cars, including 19 fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing approximately 286,000 pounds (130,000 kg) each and 14 empty tanker cars weighing about 72,000 pounds (33,000 kg) each. Most remarkably, one empty tanker car was lofted 475.5 feet (144.9 meters) south of North Dakota State Highway 46. This extraordinary train car damage became the critical evidence for the later EF5 upgrade, as wind speed calculations based on the lofting of objects this size and weight indicated winds exceeding the EF5 threshold.

Continuing north of Highway 46, the tornado caused devastating damage to homes, including one farmhouse that was completely leveled, resulting in two fatalities. The tornado then continued northward, causing extreme tree damage and completely leveling another farmhouse, which resulted in a third fatality. Along this section, the tornado completely destroyed numerous outbuildings, blew over a cellular communications tower anchored by four cables, and caused severe damage to crop fields. In the Maple River valley east of Enderlin, extensive tree damage characterized the damage path, with only stubs of large branches or trunks remaining and marked debarking exhibiting a "sandpapering" effect. Trees throughout the area displayed root ball displacements.

Near Highway 46, a farmstead sustain complete destruction with its foundation swept clean, leaving only the basement remaining with debris scattered downwind. As the tornado moved through this area, it bent over tall steel electrical transmission towers before beginning to weaken.

The tornado dissipated at 11:21 p.m. CDT north of Enderlin, having been on the ground for approximately 19 minutes. Its path length totaled 12.1 miles (19.47 kilometers), and at its maximum extent, the tornado was 1.05 miles (1.69 kilometers) wide.

### Casualties

Three people were killed in the Enderlin tornado, all residents of Enderlin and vicinity. The victims were identified as Michael Dalton Dehn and Katherine Ann Pfaff-Dehn, both 73 years old, and Marcario Machuca Lucio, 89 years old. Two fatalities occurred at one leveled farmhouse south of Highway 46, while the third death occurred at a separate farmstead north of Highway 46. The tornado resulted in multiple injuries, though the exact number was not widely reported in initial assessments.

### Damage Assessment and Rating Upgrade

The National Weather Service office in Grand Forks conducted an initial survey on June 23, 2025, three days after the event. Based on standard Enhanced Fujita Scale damage indicators, the tornado received a preliminary rating of high-end EF3 with estimated peak winds of 160 mph (260 km/h). However, meteorologist Mel Beerends of the Grand Forks office suspected the actual winds had been more powerful based on the unusual damage to the freight train.

Beerends assembled a team of wind damage experts from the National Weather Service and the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University's Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory in London, Ontario. The team, which included meteorologists Jim LaDue and Timothy P. Marshall, along with engineers Dr. Connell Miller, Dr. Greg Kopp, and Dr. David Sills, conducted extensive forensic analysis of the damage. Using engineering assessments, simulations, and damage trajectory analysis of the lofted and tipped train cars, the team determined that the wind speeds necessary to cause such damage far exceeded those estimated for an EF3 tornado.

The critical evidence came from analysis of the displaced empty tanker car. Research published by Miller and colleagues established that lofting large compact objects more than 50 meters generally indicates EF5-level winds of at least 200 mph. In the Enderlin case, a fully loaded tanker car—nearly four times heavier than the heaviest object modeled in the study—was thrown almost three times farther than the EF5 threshold distance, indicating wind speeds well above 210 mph. Additional analysis of the tipped grain hopper cars and other high-end damage indicators supported this assessment.

Based on this comprehensive analysis, the National Weather Service in Grand Forks officially upgraded the Enderlin tornado to EF5 status on October 6, 2025, with maximum winds estimated at greater than 210 miles per hour (340 kilometers per hour). This upgrade ended the longest period without an officially rated EF5 tornado in United States history, succeeding the May 20, 2013, Moore tornado in Oklahoma.

### Broader Outbreak Context

The Enderlin tornado was part of a significant and destructive weather system that affected the northern Great Plains between June 19 and 22, 2025. The broader event produced over 20 confirmed tornadoes across North Dakota, with six additional tornadoes receiving EF2 or stronger ratings. In addition to the tornadoes, a powerful derecho tracked from west to east across North Dakota during the evening and overnight hours, producing widespread wind gusts exceeding 60 mph with some locations experiencing gusts exceeding 100 mph. Very large hail, including stones up to 3 inches (76 mm) in diameter in some areas, accompanied the storms.

The storm system impacted 34 of North Dakota's 53 counties, causing widespread damage to homes, infrastructure, and the environment. Multiple train derailments occurred beyond the Enderlin event, including a Burlington Northern Santa Fe (BNSF) derailment of 43 empty coal cars near Steele due to high derecho winds, and another BNSF derailment near Mayville in Traill County where wind gusts overturned grain cars.

Power outages were extensive, with approximately 37,000 people and businesses without power at the peak of the event, affecting both southeastern North Dakota and portions of northwestern Minnesota. Prolonged power outages severely hampered emergency response and recovery operations, with over 30,500 customers affected in North Dakota and 54,600 in Minnesota at the height of the outages.

### Disaster Declaration and Recovery

On June 22, 2025, North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster following the tornado outbreak and activated the State Emergency Operations Plan. President Donald Trump approved Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) disaster relief for 19 North Dakota counties affected by the June 20–21 storms, including Cass County. The state estimated damages exceeded $11.4 million, with federal relief expectations of approximately $16 million.

However, disaster assistance distribution was complicated by timing. In early June 2025, President Trump had announced plans to phase out FEMA after the hurricane season, and a federal government shutdown began shortly after the tornado. This shutdown delayed the disbursement of federal disaster funds, leaving the affected communities without immediate federal assistance despite the disaster declaration. The Department of Emergency Services and state officials continued preparing reimbursement requests during the shutdown for submission once government operations resumed.

Local response efforts began immediately after the tornado. Cass County Emergency Manager Brady Scribner reported significant damage to agricultural sites and farmsteads, with destroyed grain bins, irrigation systems, and power lines affecting rural operations. The community of Enderlin and surrounding areas received support from various volunteer organizations and mutual aid efforts. A whole community response emerged, with volunteers and private partners stepping in to assist with damage removal, debris clearing, and damage assessment efforts. The Small Business Administration also offered relief programs to North Dakota businesses and nonprofits affected by the June storm.

### Historical Significance

The 2025 Enderlin tornado holds several historical records. It was the first EF5 tornado to occur in the United States since May 20, 2013, ending a 12-year period without such high-intensity tornadoes. It was also the first EF5 or F5 tornado to occur in North Dakota in exactly 68 years, the last being the devastating Fargo tornado of June 20, 1957, which killed 10 people. The Enderlin tornado was the deadliest tornado in North Dakota since the July 4, 1978, F4 tornado near Elgin, which killed five people, though the Elgin tornado had greater fatalities.

The tornado's classification relied on new methodologies in forensic meteorological analysis. The use of debris trajectory calculations from the lofted train cars to determine wind speeds represented an application of cutting-edge research that had been validated by the Northern Tornadoes Project. This methodology proved crucial because the Enderlin tornado lacked the extensive structural damage to buildings typical of earlier EF5 tornadoes, as much of its path consisted of open fields and agricultural areas with scattered farmsteads.

Published on May 26, 2021

After a few hours sleep in the car, just north of Englewood, Kansas, I woke early, around 4:30AM, so I could find a spot to photograph the lunar eclipse at sunrise. I headed north and found a wind farm about six miles south of Minneola. It seemed like a unique way to kick start what I hoped would be a robust chase day.

![Image 1](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5169_1920px.jpg)

Almost fully eclipsed Moon setting into the wind turbines — 1102Z

*   ![Image 2](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5092-Edit_1280px.jpg)
    
*   ![Image 3](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5111-Edit_1280px.jpg)
    

Tighter shots as the eclipse progressed — 1005Z and 1042Z

As the Moon disappeared into full eclipse, convection was already bustling on the eastern horizon as approaching sunrise silhouetted the towers and turbines. As the sun crested the horizon, the storm tops sculpted a great display of crepuscular rays. It was a beautiful thing to see, and worth the early start.

![Image 4](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5128_1280px.jpg)

![Image 5](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5207_1280px.jpg)

*   ![Image 6](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5220_1280px.jpg)
    
*   ![Image 7](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5241_1280px.jpg)
    

My chase target for the day was the dryline in far western Kansas. I was hoping for an isolated storm in that area rather than chasing a thicker bunch of storms on the warm front further north. My biggest concern was that a clean, isolated cell would lead to chaser logjams, so I was trying to prep for staying out of the mess as much as possible and hoping the unpaved grid had dried off enough to stay off the paved pain points.

Speaking of dried off enough, I was at my target south of Scott City early enough to do some maintenance on my wheels. The mud road adventure a couple days earlier was making for a very rough ride. I purchased small pry bar, found a remote dirt road, and went to work chipping all the dried on mud out of the wheel rims and everywhere else it was packed in. That made a huge difference in getting my smooth ride back.

Not long after 21Z, convection was firing on the dryline directly to the west. Strong storms were already bustling on the warm front, but this looked like the one I was hoping for.

![Image 8](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2133_1280px.jpg)

Convective initiation looking directly west from four miles south of Scott City — 2125Z

I took off after it as it drifted north and strengthened. The anvil was stretching straight overhead and I was pretty excited to run with this one on a good road network.

![Image 9](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5246_1280px.jpg)

Strengthening cell from seven miles north of Scott City — 2201Z

I headed west and north to get closer and wound through some interesting landscape in the drainage north of Pence. The cell was splitting and the left split was looking stronger on radar while the right one seemed to be diminishing. I wasn’t going to try and run after the left one. The right one still had a decently sculpted look to it and I hoped it would recharge.

![Image 10](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2143_1280px.jpg)

Cell that I hoped would gather its wits after a split — 2224Z

The cap was determined to smother this storm and dashed my hopes for it. So after some parting shots, I let it go and headed back to Highway 83 to try and salvage something with storms further north.

![Image 11](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5256_1280px.jpg)

Withering cell with some strange sandstone outcrops three miles south of Little Jerusalem Badlands State Park — 2245Z

![Image 12](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2156_1280px.jpg)

Parting shot over a crumbling structure — 2254Z

About an hour and a half later, up east of Hoxie, I was catching up to a new batch of development and worked my way further east and then north. Storms were ongoing and developing all around me, but were spaced enough apart to be able to avoid hail and get some clear shots along the way.

*   ![Image 13](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5266_1280px.jpg)
    
    From 10 miles east of Hoxie, KS — 0032Z
    
*   ![Image 14](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5269_1280px.jpg)
    
    From two miles west of Penokee looking northwest — 0053Z
    
*   ![Image 15](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2173-Edit_1280px.jpg)
    
    Same spot looking south — 0054Z
    

Terrain was a challenge in places and a couple miles West of Penokee, I took a gamble on an unpaved road that had been freshly rained on so that I could get a hill crest vantage. It seemed a bit slick on the way up, but not too bad and it offered a great view for a while. The trip back down the hill was sobering. Gravity threatened to turn every slight nuance of braking and turning into a slow sideways glide into the ditch. After successfully getting back to the paved road, I committed to staying off the dirt roads in this freshly soaked area.

![Image 16](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2176_1280px.jpg)

View from a slick hill crest two miles west of Penokee — 0055Z

The cell I was following gradually shriveled away as I paced it north of Hill City. I detached and tried to see if storms coming up from the south would do any better. But that turned into a mess, being on the wrong sides of the cells and not wanting to core punch or get out on the grid for better angles. So I headed further north to get in the clear and try for some twilight shots.

*   ![Image 17](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2184_1280px.jpg)
    
    From 11 miles north of Hill City — 0116Z
    
*   ![Image 18](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2189_1280px.jpg)
    
    Finally shriveling up from 12 miles south of Norton — 0128Z
    

A couple miles west of Norton, I found a spot with a good view of a trio of stronger cells spinning away in the clear as twilight deepened. So I set up cameras on both of them and snagged time lapses with some beautiful structure and lightning. The day didn’t serve up what I had hoped for, but getting shots of several supercells and twilight lightning was still a success.

![Image 19](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2192_1280px.jpg)

Mammatus sunset, looking south from two miles west of Norton, Kansas — 0208Z

![Image 20](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-IMG_2321_1280px.jpg)

Cell to the southeast — 0221Z

*   ![Image 21](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5360_1280px.jpg)
    
    0214Z
    
*   ![Image 22](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5736_1280px.jpg)
    
    0229Z
    

Ceaseless lightning display on the cell to the northwest

![Image 23](https://highwaysandhailstones.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/img20210526-R5__5864_1280px.jpg)

Layered structure and lightning on that northwest cell — 0237Z

I was originally planning to get a hotel for the night, but gave up on that option and just boondocked again south of Plainville so I could save time and grab as much sleep as possible before a long drive the next day deep into the Texas Panhandle.

A couple cell phone videos of the lightning display posted during the chase are below.

Lightning display in multiple directions from Norton, Kansas is sublime.

By[TW](https://watchers.news/author/tw/) Tuesday, August 2, 2016Wednesday, September 25, 2024

Featured image: Landslide in Nepal on July 27, 2016. Credit: eKantipur

According to the Monsoon Preparedness Assessment 2016 carried out by Shelter Cluster Nepal, as many as 18 287 households in 14 districts of Nepal most affected by the massive [M8.1 earthquake last year](https://watchers.news/tag/gorkha-earthquake/) are living under high landslide hazard risks. The earthquake triggered more than 4 000 landslides in earthquake-affected and adjoining districts.

Sindhupalchok has the highest number of households at 5 267 that are at high risk of landslide hazard followed by Dhading (3 585), Gorkha (2 814), Kavre (2 409), Makawanpur (1 152),  Rasuwa (1 039) and Sindhuli (881). In total, about 91 433 individuals are living under high landslide hazard.

In addition, 28 608 households in 14 districts have been listed as living under moderate risk to landslide hazards. In total, this is 143 320 individuals living under moderate risk.

![Image 6](https://watchers.news/wp-content/uploads/GSC%20-%20nepal%20-%20aug2016%20-%20landslide%20risk%20map(1).jpg)

31 476 households, or 157 378 individuals, are living in districts under flood hazard.

![Image 7](https://watchers.news/wp-content/uploads/GSC%20-%20nepal%20-%20aug2016%20-%20flood%20risk%20map.jpg)

The assessment also found that 46 894 households are living below the poverty line in temporary shelters or collective sites. They are most likely to need assistance in the event of monsoon impacts. Poorer families are particularly likely to be living in low quality shelters that are unable to withstand heavy winds, and generally lack access to land that is safe from landslide and flooding.

The Central Disaster Relief Committee (CDRC) for disaster management, under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MoHA), said at least 102 people have died in over three months from floods and landslides in 42 districts.

Pyuthan district was the hardest hit with 31 deaths so far.
